sourceEvidence.label: Two owner-provided Go authentication exports and the current AviaSurveil360 identity boundary

assessment.summary: The two exports supply useful password, token, refresh-session, lifecycle, and client primitives, but replacement requires one deliberately owned identity boundary rather than direct integration of either persistence model or protocol claim.

constraints.profile: security-first within one ARM64 t4g.small private pilot
nonNegotiables: Preserve immutable provider subject identity and exact organization isolation.
Retain the current same-origin BFF, HttpOnly session, CSRF, and fail-closed application authorization boundaries.
Do not accept ambiguous fallback between Keycloak and first-party token issuers.
Do not implement cryptographic or OAuth/OIDC protocol primitives without a maintained reviewed library.
Keep Keycloak available until parity, migration, recovery, and rollback gates pass.
assumptions: The repository owner has authority to reuse and modify the exported first-party application sources.
No measured replacement-service ARM64 memory or latency evidence exists yet.
WebAuthn is optional for the first cutover; TOTP and hashed recovery codes are mandatory.

opportunities.title: Replace Keycloak without collapsing authentication into application authorization
opportunities.summary: Use selected source concepts and tests in a standards-conforming, separately privileged Go OIDC provider while AviaSurveil360 retains application sessions, memberships, and organization authorization.
opportunities.diagnosis: The imported sources combine useful native credential/session mechanics with proprietary token protocols. One has an unrelated user/permission schema; the other stores security state through unsafe full-row DynamoDB updates and has no tenant model. Direct integration would duplicate or omit AviaSurveil360 authority and weaken the current OIDC, concurrency, and tenant boundaries.

evidence.claim: The export records missing OIDC, MFA, recovery, organization isolation, account-state, throttling, and complete audit controls.
AviaSurveil360 already owns encrypted server-side browser sessions, CSRF, authority observation, and bounded session lifetimes.
The current API consumes Authorization Code plus PKCE OIDC and requires exact issuer, nonce, organization, role, and email claims.
Selected password and refresh-family mechanics can seed a new provider, but the exported store and tables should not become AviaSurveil360's application authorization authority.

The Kindred export records non-atomic refresh rotation, cross-account logout denial of service, password-change session survival, stale full-row writes, missing key rotation, inconsistent verification gates, incomplete throttling, and stale WebSocket sessions.
RS256 negative tests, lifecycle cases, and client refresh serialization can inform Avia-owned code, but the DynamoDB store and discovery facade must not enter the replacement runtime.

desiredInvariants: Authentication establishes one immutable subject; application authorization resolves one exact active organization membership server-side.
Only a standards-conforming issuer URL emits OIDC discovery, authorization codes, ID tokens, and JWKS.
Password change, suspension, MFA reset, refresh reuse, and deactivation revoke every affected credential and application session fail closed.
Credential, MFA, signing-key, and SMTP authority is unavailable to normal application and worker code.
Keycloak and the replacement never share an issuer and are never accepted through fallback verification.

options.title: Retain and harden Keycloak
options.summary: Keep the current provider and close only its image, resource, and operational gaps.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: The first candidate is not integrated.
The second candidate is not integrated.
Existing provider parity is preserved, but image and operational hardening remain.

tradeoffs.assessment: Mature OIDC and MFA behavior stays intact, while the imported defects remain unreachable.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Rerun realm, MFA, session, dependency, and recovery gates.

tradeoffs.assessment: The current login path and service hop remain.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure login and refresh latency on native ARM64.

tradeoffs.assessment: The JVM and Keycloak runtime remain the dominant identity footprint.
Known provider behavior and recovery tooling remain available.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run restart, database-loss, SMTP-loss, and session-revocation drills.

tradeoffs.assessment: Existing realm, patch, database, and JVM operations remain.
No subject or credential migration is required.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Confirm no replacement paths enter runtime builds.

residualRisks: Keycloak resource and dependency burden remains on the t4g.small host.

acceptanceCriteria: Existing OIDC/TOTP and capacity gates pass.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Retain the previous reviewed immutable Keycloak subject.

options.title: Embed native identity and OIDC into the API
options.summary: Place credentials, MFA, OIDC endpoints, and application APIs in one Go process.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: Every first-export control must be rewritten or adapted in the API.
Every second-export concurrency, revocation, protocol, throttling, and lifecycle control must be rewritten or adapted in the API.
Existing BFF and membership controls can be reused, but privilege concentration increases.

tradeoffs.assessment: An API compromise would gain password verification, MFA secrets, and issuer signing authority.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Threat-model secret and database authority reachable from every API handler.

tradeoffs.assessment: One process removes the provider network hop.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Benchmark login, callback, and ordinary API latency.

tradeoffs.assessment: No separate provider process is retained.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure peak RSS under mixed API, Argon2id, PDF, and worker load.

tradeoffs.assessment: API deployment or failure also removes login and recovery availability.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run restart and partial-dependency fault tests.

tradeoffs.assessment: One fewer service and database role simplifies supervision.
OIDC, credentials, application sessions, and authorization evolve in one high-conflict codebase.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Prototype package boundaries and review secret access at compile time.

residualRisks: Credential and signing authority shares the main API blast radius.

workPackages: Implement all identity capabilities inside the API.
acceptanceCriteria: Full protocol, lifecycle, tenant, and security parity passes.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Route login back to Keycloak and restore the previous API image while the old provider database remains intact.

options.title: Build a separately privileged first-party Go OIDC provider
options.summary: Use selected native primitives behind a maintained OIDC library in a small dedicated service and keep application authorization in AviaSurveil360.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: Reported credential, session, lifecycle, audit, and authorization gaps become explicit work packages.
Reported refresh, logout, password, stale-write, key, verification, throttling, and long-lived-session gaps become explicit regression work.
Existing OIDC/BFF and membership controls remain while Keycloak-specific administration is replaced behind an interface.
TOTP, recovery, subject, organization, and lifecycle invariants are acceptance gates.

tradeoffs.assessment: Credential, MFA, and signing authority stays outside normal API and worker code, while standards behavior comes from a reviewed library.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Threat-model, test every imported finding, and obtain an independent security review before cutover.

tradeoffs.assessment: A local provider hop remains, but Go startup and request overhead should be smaller than the current JVM; no measurement exists.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Benchmark authorization, token, refresh, admin, and JWKS paths on ARM64.

tradeoffs.assessment: A small Go provider should use less memory than Keycloak, but Argon2id concurrency and caches can still exhaust the host.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure steady and peak RSS with bounded Argon2id concurrency under the complete mixed workload.

tradeoffs.assessment: Identity retains failure isolation, but the project assumes responsibility for protocol and recovery behavior.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run crash, restart, database, key rotation, SMTP, clock-skew, and refresh-reuse drills.

tradeoffs.assessment: The team owns a new security-critical provider, migrations, keys, mail, monitoring, and incident runbooks.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Review on-call, backup, restore, rotation, and break-glass procedures.

tradeoffs.assessment: Provider admin callers, identity state, credentials, factors, issuer routing, and rollback need explicit migration.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run a synthetic shadow migration and prove exact subject retention and rollback before any cutover.

residualRisks: The team becomes the operator of a security-critical identity provider.
OIDC library correctness does not supply application-specific lifecycle, tenant, MFA, mail, audit, or migration correctness.

workPackages: Follow the separate Auth Replacement ExecPlan.
acceptanceCriteria: All parity, conformance, security, migration, recovery, and ARM64 gates pass before Keycloak removal.
migrationNotes: Retain exact subjects; do not migrate passwords or MFA secrets without a separately reviewed safe mechanism.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Keep Keycloak data and immutable images until post-cutover acceptance; route the exact issuer back and invalidate replacement sessions.

opportunities.recommendation: Use the separate Go provider because it can reduce the Keycloak footprint without giving the ordinary API credential and signing authority. Keep Keycloak as the serving provider until every gate passes.

openQuestions: Which maintained Go authorization-server library passes the required local interoperability spike and has acceptable maintenance and licensing?
Should the first cutover support only TOTP and recovery codes, with WebAuthn deferred, or is passkey support mandatory?
Are there any non-synthetic Keycloak subjects at cutover time that require credential or factor migration rather than invitation-based re-enrollment?
